slides.0.title: Rosé, Sweet Wines, Sparkling and Outlying Regions
slides.0.subtitle: Tavel, VDN, Die and outlying names
slides.1.title: Where the rosé is
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Tavel: the specialist
slides.1.highlights.0.content: The Rhône's only cru devoted to rosé (1936); Grenache blended with several main varieties, Grenache noir required in the blend; about 781 ha in 2025
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Lirac and Côtes du Rhône
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Lirac rosé shares the red rules (Grenache at least 40%, Syrah + Mourvèdre at least 25%) and was only about 2% of its 2025 volume; Côtes du Rhône was about 8% rosé in 2025, the whole valley about 14%
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Big rosé in the outlying names
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Rosé share in 2025: Luberon about 51%, Costières de Nîmes about 48%, Ventoux about 35%, Côtes du Vivarais about 33% (Inter Rhône)
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Rosé in Laudun and Cairanne?
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Inter Rhône's 2025 table still shows about 31% rosé for Laudun and 7% for Cairanne, yet their specifications list only red and white (probably transition or reporting basis; unconfirmed). Their colour lists are therefore not tested
slides.1.content: Rosé comes in two forms: specialists like Tavel, and large-volume production in the outlying appellations.
slides.2.title: Vins doux naturels (VDN)
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Decree of 1 June 1945; Muscat à petits grains (white and red) from Aubignan and Beaumes-de-Venise; yield 30 hl of must/ha (ceiling 40); natural must sugar at least 252 g/L
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Fortification (mutage)
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Neutral spirit of at least 96% vol. is added during fermentation, at 5–10% of the must volume, halting it and keeping the natural sugar; the rule is the same as for Rasteau VDN
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Colour and share
slides.2.highlights.2.content: The Muscat VDN may be white, rosé or red; white was about 82% of volume in Inter Rhône 2025, on about 227 ha. The INAO text said about 95% white in 2009 — different years, not tested
slides.2.highlights.3.title: Rasteau VDN and ageing terms
slides.2.highlights.3.content: Rasteau VDN is only about 18 ha (2025). Drive notes: ambré/tuilé need at least 3 years' ageing, hors d'âge 5 years, while blanc/grenat are fresher (release after 1 May of the following year) — the periods were not checked against INAO and are not tested
slides.2.content: Both VDN are fortified to keep sugar; Hermitage vin de paille is a different route to sweetness.
slides.3.title: Sparkling wines of the Diois
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Clairette de Die
slides.3.highlights.0.content: First recognised as an appellation of origin in 1910, an AOC by decree of 30 December 1942, with two production methods distinguished by the decree of 25 May 1971. About 1,355 ha in 2025
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Méthode dioise ancestrale
slides.3.highlights.1.content: At least 75% Muscat à petits grains (white version); a single fermentation finishing in the bottle with no tirage or expedition liqueur; at least 4 months on lees in bottle; about 88% of Diois output
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Second fermentation in bottle
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Fully fermented wine is bottled with tirage liqueur and aged at least 9 months on lees, Clairette only; about 7% of output. Crémant de Die was defined by the decree of 26 March 1993 and covers about 64 ha in 2025
slides.3.highlights.3.title: Others
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Châtillon-en-Diois draws on Gamay, Aligoté and Chardonnay (no percentages in the INAO document); Saint-Péray's sparkling wine is in lesson 4
slides.3.content: The "ancestrale" method of Die is not the traditional method: it is a single fermentation finished in the bottle.
slides.4.title: The outlying appellations and what counts as "Rhône"
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Ventoux
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Recognised as Côtes du Ventoux on 27 July 1973 and renamed Ventoux by decree of 17 October 2009; 53 communes in the Vaucluse; red, rosé and white; about 4,987 ha in 2025 (54% red, 35% rosé, 11% white)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Luberon
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Recognised as Côtes du Luberon on 26 February 1988 and renamed Luberon on 18 September 2009; the INAO text gives 36 communes in the Vaucluse; about 2,781 ha in 2025 (rosé about 51%)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Grignan-les-Adhémar and others
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Grignan-les-Adhémar was formerly Coteaux du Tricastin; Drive notes say the old name lasted until 2010 (renamed over the nuclear-plant image). About 971 ha in 2025. Côtes du Vivarais about 120 ha, Costières de Nîmes about 2,145 ha
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Three ways to draw "Rhône"
slides.4.highlights.3.content: (1) the core of 18 crus, Villages and Côtes du Rhône; (2) Inter Rhône's statistical scope, adding Ventoux, Luberon, Grignan-les-Adhémar, Costières de Nîmes, Vivarais and the Diois; (3) the geographic valley. Costières de Nîmes is in the Gard next to Languedoc but sits under the Rhône committee (since 2004). None of the outlying names is one of the 18 crus
slides.4.content: For border cases, say first which definition of "Rhône" you are using.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
Which grape is used for Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise?
Only Muscat à petits grains (white and red) is permitted.
What characterises Clairette de Die's "méthode dioise ancestrale"?
A. Mostly Muscat à petits grains, with a single fermentation finished in bottle
B. 100% Chardonnay with a dosed second fermentation
C. Fermentation stopped with fortifying spirit
At least 75% Muscat à petits grains (white version), a single fermentation finished in bottle, no tirage or expedition liqueur.
Recognised as Côtes du Ventoux in 1973 and renamed Ventoux in 2009. Coteaux du Tricastin is the former name of Grignan-les-Adhémar.
Which of these is NOT one of the 18 Côtes du Rhône crus?
Ventoux is an outlying AOC outside the 18 crus; Tavel, Lirac and Laudun are crus.
